threads.thread_goal: Align on current workflow, main issues, and project scope before design work.

messages.text: Hi everyone, welcome to the outpatient check-in and triage rollout project. We have 21 days to design and implement a standardized process that reduces waiting times and improves data quality. Let's start by mapping what we do today. Can each of you share how check-in and triage currently work in your area, and what the main pain points are? This will help us build A1 (Current vs Future Outpatient Check-in Workflow Map) and complete T1 (Map current outpatient check-in and triage workflow across shifts). Looking forward to hearing from the team.

Thanks for kicking this off. From the nursing side, triage is currently done after patients check in at the desk. We assess vital signs and chief complaint, but the criteria for escalation aren't always clear. Sometimes we have to ask the front desk to repeat information because it wasn't captured properly on the intake form. I think we need a clearer protocol and better handoff between desk and nursing.

From the front desk, we're juggling paper forms, the EHR, and phone calls. Patients often don't fill out forms completely, so we end up asking them again. During busy shifts, check-in can take 10-15 minutes per patient. We also don't have a standard way to handle consent or data protection questions. Forms are only in English right now, which is a barrier for some patients.

Quality perspective: we don't have a consistent audit routine for check-in and triage. I've noticed data inconsistencies between paper intake and the EHR, and we're not tracking incidents or improvement ideas systematically. This is where T4 (Design quality control checklist for daily process audits) and T12 (Create incident and improvement log for the new process) will be critical.

I can help with the forms and documentation side. We need to make sure the new intake forms are clear and capture all mandatory fields without being too long. I'm thinking we should also align with the EHR fields early on, so there's no duplicate entry. That's part of T6 (Align new workflow with existing EHR data entry steps), right?

From a training and documentation perspective, I'll need to understand the final workflow before I can create materials. But I'm already thinking about how to structure T5 (Create staff training materials for front-desk and nursing teams) and T10 (Document final standard operating procedure for check-in and triage) so they're clear and accessible for different shifts.

Great input, everyone. So the main issues are: unclear triage criteria, data duplication, long check-in times, language barriers, and no systematic QC. Before we design the new process, we need to agree on what success looks like. I'm proposing we focus on: (1) reducing average check-in time to under 8 minutes, (2) 100% data accuracy between intake and EHR, (3) clear escalation paths for nursing, and (4) compliance with data protection. Does this align with what you're seeing?

Those metrics make sense. On the triage side, I'd add that we need clear criteria for what constitutes urgent vs routine, and a documented escalation path. I can help draft that as part of T3 (Define triage protocol and escalation criteria for outpatient visits).

I agree with those metrics. For quality control, I'd suggest we also track incident frequency and resolution time. That way we can measure if the new process is actually reducing errors. We'll need to define what counts as an incident and how we'll log it.

I support those goals. One thing I want to flag: we need to make sure the new process doesn't disrupt appointments during core hours. The constraint says no disruption, so we'll need to be careful about when we pilot and how we roll out. Maybe we start with off-peak hours?

Good point. We should also confirm which parts of the current workflow we want to keep. For example, do we keep the current EHR data entry sequence, or do we redesign that too? I think we need to decide what stays and what changes before we design the new forms.

Excellent question. Let me propose D2: we keep the existing EHR system and data entry structure as-is for now, but we optimize the sequence and remove duplicate steps. We also keep the current appointment scheduling system. What we're redesigning is the intake forms, the triage protocol, and the handoff between front desk and nursing. Does that work for everyone?
That works for me. It means we can focus on the workflow and forms without getting bogged down in EHR customization. I'll start drafting the triage protocol based on our current clinical guidelines.

Agreed. That scope is manageable. Now, for T1, I think we should document the current workflow by shift and day, so we capture all the variations. That will help us design a process that works across all shifts.

Good idea. So here's what I'm hearing: we have clear success metrics (D1), we know what stays and what changes (D2), and we're ready to start mapping the current workflow (T1) and drafting the new forms (T2), triage protocol (T3), and QC checklist (T4). I'll coordinate T1 with the team. Can someone take the lead on T2 and T3?

I can take T2 (Draft standardized patient intake and consent forms in two languages). I'll start with the current form and identify what's missing or redundant. I'll also make sure we have consent language that covers data protection.
I'll take T3 (Define triage protocol and escalation criteria for outpatient visits). I'll draft the categories and escalation paths based on our clinical guidelines and get feedback from the team.

I'll take T4 (Design quality control checklist for daily process audits). I'll create a checklist that covers the key steps and includes compliance and data accuracy checks. I'll also define pass/fail criteria.

Perfect. So we have: T1 (workflow mapping) with me, T2 (forms) with 196511, T3 (triage protocol) with 313168, and T4 (QC checklist) with 437517. Let's aim to have drafts ready by EOD tomorrow so we can review them in TH2. Everyone good with that timeline?

Sounds good. I'll help with T1 by documenting the current front-desk workflow and pain points. I can also help with T7 (Plan and schedule staff training sessions across shifts) once we have the new process defined.

I'll be ready to start on T5 and T10 once the workflow and forms are finalized. I'll also help with T11 (Prepare communication to patients about new check-in process) to make sure the patient-facing text is clear and available in two languages.

Excellent. So to summarize TH1: we've agreed on success metrics (D1), confirmed scope (D2), and assigned initial tasks. Next thread (TH2) will focus on reviewing the drafts and making decisions on forms and triage protocol. Let's keep the momentum going!

threads.thread_goal: Design and validate the new workflow, forms, and triage protocol.

messages.text: Good morning, team. I've compiled the workflow mapping from yesterday's input and created a draft of A1 (Current vs Future Outpatient Check-in Workflow Map). I can see the main bottlenecks: duplicate data entry, unclear triage handoff, and language barriers. Now let's review the drafts from 196511, 313168, and 437517. Can you each share your initial drafts for A2 (Standardized Patient Intake and Consent Forms), A3 (Outpatient Triage Protocol and Escalation Guide), and the QC checklist?

I've drafted A2 with the following structure: patient demographics, insurance info, chief complaint, current medications, allergies, and consent for data processing. I included mandatory fields and made the form concise. I also prepared a version in Spanish. The form is designed to fit on one page to reduce check-in time. Can you review for clinical relevance and data protection compliance?

The form looks good overall. I'd suggest adding a field for 'reason for visit' and 'previous visits to this clinic' so we have context for triage. Also, the consent language should explicitly mention that we'll use the data for clinical care and quality improvement. I'll review the clinical relevance more carefully once I finalize A3.

From a quality perspective, the form is clear. I'd add a field for 'date of last visit' to help with data consistency checks. Also, make sure the consent section is prominent so staff can't miss it during audit.

I've drafted A3 (Outpatient Triage Protocol and Escalation Guide). I've defined three triage categories: routine (non-urgent), urgent (needs assessment within 30 minutes), and emergent (immediate assessment). Escalation paths are: routine to standard queue, urgent to priority queue, emergent to on-call provider. I've aligned this with our existing clinical guidelines.

Good structure. Can you clarify the criteria for each category? For example, what symptoms or vital signs trigger 'urgent' vs 'routine'? We need specific, measurable criteria so all nurses apply the protocol consistently.

Good point. I'll add specific criteria: routine = stable vitals, no acute symptoms; urgent = elevated vitals, acute pain, or concerning symptoms that need assessment within 30 minutes; emergent = severe pain, altered mental status, or vital sign abnormalities requiring immediate intervention. I'll refine this with clinical guidelines and share an updated version.

I've drafted the QC checklist with items covering: form completion (all mandatory fields filled), consent signature present, vital signs recorded, triage category assigned, escalation path documented, and data entry in EHR completed. I've defined pass/fail criteria: 100% compliance on mandatory fields and consent, 95% accuracy on vital signs and triage assignment.

Solid checklist. I'd suggest adding a check for 'language preference documented' since we're rolling out bilingual forms. Also, maybe a spot check on data consistency between paper form and EHR entry. That ties into T6 (Align new workflow with existing EHR data entry steps).

Good additions. I'll add those checks. Now, who's going to own T6 (Align new workflow with existing EHR data entry steps)? We need to make sure the new intake process feeds cleanly into the EHR without duplication.

I can take T6. I'll map the new form fields to the EHR fields and identify any gaps or overlaps. I'll also document the sequence of data entry steps so front-desk staff know exactly what to do and in what order.

Perfect. So we have drafts for A2, A3, and the QC checklist. Before we finalize, I need to confirm: are we ready to approve the structure and mandatory fields of A2 (D3)? And are we ready to approve A3 and the escalation criteria (D4)?

I'm ready to approve A2 once 196511 adds the 'reason for visit' and 'date of last visit' fields. For A3, I need to finalize the specific criteria for each triage category, which I'll do today. Then we can approve.
I'm ready to approve A2 with those additions. For A3, I need to see the specific triage criteria before I sign off. Once I have that, I can confirm the QC checklist aligns with the protocol.
From the front-desk perspective, A2 looks good. The one-page format will help with check-in speed. I'm also ready to approve once the fields are finalized.
I'll add those fields to A2 today. I'll also make sure the form is still one page and the language is clear. I'll send the updated version by EOD.
I'll finalize A3 with specific triage criteria by EOD as well. Once I share it, we can make the final decision on D4.

Great. So by EOD today, we'll have updated versions of A2 and A3. Tomorrow morning, we'll review and finalize D3 and D4. In the meantime, 196511 will work on T6 to align the forms with EHR fields. Does that work?

Sounds good. I'll also refine the QC checklist based on the final A3 criteria. Once we have D3 and D4 locked in, we can move forward with T8 (Run pilot of new check-in and triage process for selected time window) planning.
Perfect. Let's reconvene tomorrow morning to finalize D3 and D4. Once those are locked, we'll have a solid foundation for the rest of the project. Great work, team.

threads.thread_goal: Define quality control approach and how audits and incidents will be handled.

messages.text: Hi team, now that we have the workflow and forms locked in, let's focus on quality control. I've prepared a draft of A4 (Daily Check-in and Triage Quality Control Checklist) and a template for A6 (Pilot Metrics and Incident Log). The checklist covers form completion, consent, vital signs, triage assignment, and EHR data entry. The incident log will track errors, near-misses, and improvement suggestions. Let me know your thoughts.

Good start. I have a few questions: How often will we run the audits? Daily? Per shift? And who will be responsible for each shift? We need to make sure the audit routine is sustainable and doesn't add too much burden to the team.

Good question. I'm proposing daily audits, but not on every patient. Instead, we do a spot check on 10% of check-ins per shift. That's manageable and still gives us good coverage. For responsibility, I suggest the QC person (me) does the morning shift, and we assign a trained staff member to do afternoon and evening shifts. We'll rotate to avoid burnout.

That sounds reasonable. But I want to make sure the audit criteria are clear so different people apply them consistently. Can you add specific examples to the checklist? For instance, what counts as 'complete' for the consent field?

Absolutely. I'll add examples and definitions to the checklist. For consent, 'complete' means: signature present, date filled in, and patient initials on data processing clause. I'll do the same for other fields.
I can help with the afternoon shift audits. I'm already here during those hours, and I can do a quick spot check without disrupting the workflow. Just need clear instructions on what to look for.

Great, thanks. I'll prepare a one-page quick-reference guide for the checklist so it's easy to use during a shift. Now, for the incident log (A6), I'm proposing we track: incident type (error, near-miss, delay), description, impact, root cause, and suggested fix. We'll review the log twice a week to identify patterns.

I like that structure. But I want to make sure we're not just logging incidents; we need to act on them. So for D6, I'm proposing: we review the log twice a week, identify the top 2-3 issues, and assign someone to fix them within 48 hours if possible. Does that work?

Perfect. That keeps us agile and responsive. I'll add a 'status' field to the log so we can track whether an issue is open, in progress, or resolved. We'll also document the fix so we can learn from it.

I agree. Quick fixes are important, especially during the pilot. If we see a pattern of triage errors, for example, we can adjust the protocol or provide additional coaching to the nurse doing the triage.
This approach makes sense. I'd also suggest we track 'time to resolve' for each issue so we can measure how quickly we're fixing problems. That's a good metric for the post-pilot retrospective.

Good idea. I'll add that to the log template. Now, for T9 (Set up daily quality audit routine using checklist) and T12 (Create incident and improvement log for the new process), I'll have both ready by tomorrow. The checklist will be simple and the log will be in a shared spreadsheet so everyone can access it.

Excellent. So to summarize D5: we'll do daily spot checks on 10% of check-ins per shift, with 437517 on mornings, 438229 on afternoons, and we'll assign someone for evenings. For D6: we'll review the incident log twice a week, prioritize top issues, and aim to resolve them within 48 hours. Everyone agree?
I agree. I'll also make sure the triage protocol is clear enough that we can identify triage-related issues quickly. If we see patterns, I can adjust the protocol or provide coaching.

Great. I'll finalize A4 and A6 by EOD today with all the refinements we discussed. I'll also prepare the quick-reference guide for the checklist and a training document on how to use the incident log.
Perfect. Once we have A4 and A6 finalized, we can move to TH4 to plan the training and pilot. We're making great progress. Let's keep this momentum going.

threads.thread_goal: Plan training, communication, and pilot rollout details.

messages.text: Hi team, now that we have the workflow, forms, triage protocol, and QC approach finalized, let's plan the training and pilot. I've started drafting A5 (Staff Training Deck and Quick-Reference Sheets) and A7 (Standard Operating Procedure for Outpatient Check-in and Triage). I'm also working on A8 (Patient-Facing Communication Text and Poster Layout). Before I finalize these, I need to understand the pilot timeline and scope. When are we planning to start the pilot, and which shifts or time windows will we cover?

Good question. We have 21 days total, and we've used about 5 days so far on design and planning. I'm proposing we start the pilot in 3 days (day 8), run it for 5 days (days 8-12), and then do a full rollout starting day 13. For scope, I suggest we pilot during off-peak hours first—maybe 2-4 PM on weekdays—to minimize disruption. Does that work?

That timeline is tight but doable. For the pilot, I'd suggest we include at least one morning shift so we can test the process during busier times. Maybe 2-4 PM on days 8-10, and 9-11 AM on days 11-12?

That makes sense. We'll get a better picture of how the process works under different conditions. I'll make sure the QC checklist is ready to use from day 8, and I'll personally monitor the pilot to catch any issues early.
I like the off-peak start. That gives us a chance to work out the kinks before we go live during busy hours. I'll make sure the front-desk team is ready for day 8.

Got it. So pilot is days 8-12, with off-peak and some morning hours. That means I need to have A5 (training materials) and A7 (SOP) ready by day 7 at the latest. I'll also need to coordinate with 438229 on T7 (Plan and schedule staff training sessions across shifts) to make sure everyone is trained before day 8.

I can take T7 (Plan and schedule staff training sessions across shifts). I'll coordinate with 435140 on the training materials and schedule sessions for days 5-7 so everyone is trained before the pilot. I'll also make sure we have backup staff trained in case someone is absent.

Perfect. So for D7, I'm proposing: training will be delivered in short sessions (30-45 minutes) on days 5-7, covering all shifts. Materials will include the training deck (A5), quick-reference sheets, and the SOP (A7). Training will be mandatory for all front-desk and nursing staff. Does that work?
I agree. I'd also suggest we do a brief walkthrough of the triage protocol during training so nurses understand the escalation criteria. I can lead that part of the training.

Good. I'll make sure the training materials include a section on the triage protocol with examples. I'll also include a scenario exercise so people can practice the new workflow. That should help with adoption.

Excellent. Now, for patient communication (A8), we need to let patients know about the new check-in process. I'm proposing we post signs in the waiting area and send a message to patients scheduled during the pilot. Can you draft that, 435140?

I'll draft A8 with a simple message explaining the new check-in steps and why we're making the change. I'll include it in two languages and prepare both a poster and a text message version. I'll have it ready by day 6 so we can print and post before the pilot.
I'll help with posting the signs and making sure the front-desk team has the text message ready to send. We can also mention the new process when patients call to confirm appointments.

Great. So for D8, we're confirming: pilot starts day 8, runs through day 12, covers off-peak and some morning hours, and we'll communicate with patients via signs and text messages. Training happens days 5-7. Everyone ready to move forward?
I'm ready. I'll also prepare a brief coaching guide for the nurses in case they need clarification during the pilot. That way we can address issues quickly without disrupting the workflow.

I'm ready. I'll have the QC checklist and incident log ready by day 7, and I'll be on-site during the pilot to monitor and support. I'll also prepare a daily summary of any issues so we can address them quickly.
I'm ready. I'll finalize A5, A7, and A8 by day 6. I'll also prepare a post-pilot retrospective template so we can capture lessons learned and update the SOP if needed.

Perfect. So here's the final timeline: Days 1-4 (done): design and planning. Days 5-7: training and final prep. Days 8-12: pilot. Days 13-21: full rollout and monitoring. We'll do a post-pilot retrospective on day 13 to capture lessons learned. Let's make this happen!
One more thing: I'll also prepare a checklist for day 7 to make sure everything is ready for the pilot. We'll review it together to confirm we haven't missed anything.
Excellent idea. That's the pre-go-live readiness checklist. Let's plan to review it on day 7 morning so we can address any last-minute issues. Great work, team. We're on track!
